title: Review your week without chasing a streak
summary: A short planning ritual for the routines around movement, with no recovery score or clinical inference.
author: Form editorial source author (AI-assisted)

sections.heading: Make time visible
paragraphs: NHLBI’s sleep guidance emphasizes making time for sleep and keeping regular routines. A planning worksheet does not diagnose sleep problems or establish an exercise recovery prescription.

Put your expected commitments on one page, including work, caregiving, travel and time intended for sleep. The purpose is to see competing demands. This is not a scoring system, and there is no ideal-looking calendar to win.

sections.heading: Name one recurring collision
paragraphs: Choose a practical conflict you recognize: a late meeting before an early start, a lengthy commute or an unpredictable obligation. Describe it without assigning blame. Then identify which scheduling decision, if any, you can change.

Leave a note when a constraint cannot be changed. Recording that fact can be more honest than repeatedly promising a routine that depends on an unavailable resource. Ask for help where appropriate rather than using this page as medical advice.

sections.heading: Review three moments
paragraphs: Use these prompts at the beginning, middle and end of a week. Keep the review short; it is a record of planning, not a substitute for rest.
checklist: Before: what conflict can I anticipate?
During: what changed in my schedule?
After: what should I carry into the next plan?

sections.heading: Avoid turning the record into a diagnosis
paragraphs: A streak, a missed session or a difficult night does not let this page infer your health or readiness to train. This preview has no recovery model and does not collect your answers.

If sleep or other health concerns need attention, use an appropriate professional care route. This article provides original organizational prompts and clearly scoped public references, not a treatment recommendation.
